10: (10) Nature loves to hide. R. P. 34 f.
101: (101) Greater deaths win greater portions. R. P. 49 a.
102: (102) Gods and men honour those who are slain in battle. R. P. 49 a.
103: (103) Wantonness needs putting out, even more than a house on fire. R. P. 49 a.
104: (104) It is not good for men to get all they wish to get. It is sickness that makes health pleasant; evil, good; hunger, plenty; weariness, rest. R. P. 48 b.
105: (105-107) It is hard to fight with one’s heart’s desire. Whatever it wishes to get, it purchases at the cost of soul. R. P. 49 a.
108: (108, 109) It is best to hide folly; but it is hard in times of relaxation, over our cups.
11: (11) The lord whose is the oracle at Delphoi neither utters nor hides his meaning, but shows it by a sign. R. P. 30 a.
111: (111) For what thought or wisdom have they? They follow the poets and take the crowd as their teacher, knowing not that there are many bad and few good. For even the best of them choose one thing above all others, immortal glory among mortals, while most of them are glutted like beasts. R. P. 31 a.
113: (113) One is ten thousand to me, if he be the best. R. P. 31 a.
114: (114) The Ephesians would do well to hang themselves, 155every grown man of them, and leave the city to beardless lads; for they have cast out Hermodoros, the best man among them, saying, “We will have none who is best among us; if there be any such, let him be so elsewhere and among others.” R. P. 29 b.
12: (12) And the Sibyl, with raving lips uttering things mirthless, unbedizened, and unperfumed, reaches over a thousand years with her voice, thanks to the god in her. R. P. 30 a.
122: (122) There awaits men when they die such things as they look not for nor dream of. R. P. 46 d.
123: (123) ... that they rise up and become the wakeful guardians of the quick and dead. R. P. 46 d.
124: (124) Night-walkers, Magians, priests of Bakchos and priestesses of the wine-vat, mystery-mongers....
126: (126) And they pray to these images, as if one were to talk with a man’s house, knowing not what gods or heroes are. R. P. 49 a.
127: (127) For if it were not to Dionysos that they made a procession and sang the shameful phallic hymn, they would be acting most shamelessly. But Hades is the same as Dionysos 156in whose honour they go mad and keep the feast of the wine-vat. R. P. 49.
130: (129, 130) They vainly purify themselves by defiling themselves with blood, just as if one who had stepped into the mud were to wash his feet in mud. Any man who marked him doing thus, would deem him mad. R. P. 49 a.
16: (16) The learning of many things teacheth not understanding, else would it have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, and again Xenophanes and Hekataios. R. P. 31.
17: (17) Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchos, practised inquiry beyond all other men, and choosing out these writings, claimed for his own wisdom what was but a knowledge of many things and an art of mischief. R. P. 31 a.
2: (2) Though this Word is true evermore, yet men are as unable to understand it when they hear it for the first time as before they have heard it at all. For, though all things come to pass in accordance with this Word, men seem as if they had no experience of them, when they make trial of words and deeds such as I set forth, dividing each thing according to its nature and showing how it truly is. But other men know not what they are doing when awake, even as they forget what they do in sleep. R. P. 32.
20: (20) This world, which is the same for all, no one of gods or men has made; but it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, with measures kindling, and measures going out. R. P. 35.
21: (21) The transformations of Fire are, first of all, sea; and half of the sea is earth, half whirlwind. ... R. P. 35 b.
22: (22) All things are an exchange for Fire, and Fire for all things, even as wares for gold and gold for wares. R. P. 35.
23: (23) It becomes liquid sea, and is measured by the same tale as before it became earth. R. P. 39.
24: (24) Fire is want and surfeit. R. P. 36 a.
26: (26) Fire in its advance will judge and convict all things. R. P. 36 a.
29: (29) The sun will not overstep his measures; if he does, the Erinyes, the handmaids of Justice, will find him out. R. P. 39.
32: (32) The sun is new every day.
35: (35) Hesiod is most men’s teacher. Men think he knew very many things, a man who did not know day or night! They are one. R. P. 39 b.
36: (36) God is day and night, winter and summer, war and peace, surfeit and hunger; but he takes various shapes, just as fire, when it is mingled with spices, is named according to the savour of each. R. P. 39 b.
39: (39) Cold things become warm, and what is warm cools; what is wet dries, and the parched is moisted.
41: (41, 42) You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you. R. P. 33.
43: (43) Homer was wrong in saying: “Would that strife might perish from among gods and men!” He did not see that he was praying for the destruction of the universe; for, if his prayer were heard, all things would pass away.... R. P. 34 d.
44: (44) War is the father of all and the king of all; and some he has made gods and some men, some bond and some free. R. P. 34.
45: (45) Men do not know how what is at variance agrees with itself. It is an attunement of opposite tensions, like that of the bow and the lyre. R. P. 34.
47: (47) The hidden attunement is better than the open. R. P. 34.
51: (51) Asses would rather have straw than gold. R. P. 31 a.
52: (52) The sea is the purest and the impurest water. Fish can drink it, and it is good for them; to men it is undrinkable and destructive. R. P. 47 c.
57: (57) Good and ill are one. R. P. 47 c.
58: (58) Physicians who cut, burn, stab, and rack the sick, demand a fee for it which they do not deserve to get. R. P. 47 c.
59: (59) Couples are things whole and things not whole, what is drawn together and what is drawn asunder, the harmonious and the discordant. The one is made up of all things, and all things issue from the one.
60: (60) Men would not have known the name of justice if these things were not.
61: (61) To God all things are fair and good and right, but men hold some things wrong and some right. R. P. 45.
62: (62) We must know that war is common to all and strife is justice, and that all things come into being and pass away (?) through strife.
64: (64) All the things we see when awake are death, even as all we see in slumber are sleep. R. P. 42 c.
65: (65) The wise is one only. It is unwilling and willing to be called by the name of Zeus. R. P. 40.
68: (68) For it is death to souls to become water, and death to water to become earth. But water comes from earth; and from water, soul. R. P. 38.
69: (69) The way up and the way down is one and the same. R. P. 36 d.
72: (72) It is pleasure to souls to become moist. R. P. 46 c.
73: (73) A man, when he gets drunk, is led by a beardless lad, tripping, knowing not where he steps, having his soul moist. R. P. 42.
74: (74-76) The dry soul is the wisest and best. R. P. 42.
77: (77) Man is kindled and put out like a light in the night-time.
78: (78) And it is the same thing in us that is quick and dead, awake and asleep, young and old; the former are shifted and 153become the latter, and the latter in turn are shifted and become the former. R. P. 47.
8: (8) Those who seek for gold dig up much earth and find a little. R. P. 44 b.
81: (81) We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not. R. P. 33 a.
82: (82) It is a weariness to labour for the same masters and be ruled by them.
84: (84) Even the posset separates if it is not stirred.
85: (85) Corpses are more fit to be cast out than dung.
92: (92) So we must follow the common, yet the many live as if they had a wisdom of their own. R. P. 44.
93: (93) They are estranged from that with which they have most constant intercourse. R. P. 32 b.
94: (94) It is not meet to act and speak like men asleep.
95: (95) The waking have one common world, but the sleeping turn aside each into a world of his own.
97: (97) Man is called a baby by God, even as a child by a man. R. P. 45.
98: (98, 99) The wisest man is an ape compared to God, just as the most beautiful ape is ugly compared to man.
